description_full: Ermenegildo Zegna N.V., together with its subsidiaries, designs, produces, markets, and distributes luxury menswear and womenwear, children's clothing, footwear, leather goods, and other accessories worldwide. It offers luxury leisurewear, such as knitwear, jeans, jersey and shirts, fabric and leather outerwear, and accessories; formalwear, including formal suits to tuxedos, shirts, blazers, formal coats, and accessories; and leather accessories comprising sneakers and other shoes, bags, belts and small leather accessories. The company is also manufacturing and distributing eyewear, cufflinks and jewelry, beachwear, underwear, and fragrances. In addition, it offers fine jewelry, childrenswear, textile, and home design products. The company sells its products under the ZEGNA, Thom Browne, and TOM FORD FASHION brands. It serves its products through retail stores and online channels. The company was founded in 1910 and is based in Milan, Italy. Ermenegildo Zegna N.V. operates as a subsidiary of Monterubello Societa' Semplice.

financial_summary: Ermenegildo Zegna N.V. is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $3.7B market cap on $2.1B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +11% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are expanding by +3.6pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.

Returns on capital run at 18% against a 9% cost of capital, a 9-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 67% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $281M in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.06× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 2.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 0.9%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 70% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.
